The non‑tree edge \((u,v)\) must be a back‑edge, so one endpoint is an ancestor of the other.  
Because \(\text{pre}(u)<\text{pre}(v)\), the earlier‑discovered vertex \(u\) is the ancestor of \(v\). Hence  

* **II** is always true.  

Since an ancestor finishes after all of its descendants, we have \(\text{post}(v)<\text{post}(u)\); therefore **I** (\(\text{post}(u)<\text{post}(v)\)) is false.  

With \(u\) an ancestor of \(v\), the deepest common ancestor of \(u\) and \(v\) is \(u\) itself, so **III** is true.

Thus the statements that must hold are II and III.

**Final answer: D**
